name: Snell's Law
statement: Light bends when crossing between media by an amount set by their refractive indices.
meaning: When light passes from one transparent medium into another of different optical density, it changes direction at the boundary. Entering a denser medium it bends toward the perpendicular; entering a thinner one it bends away. The refractive indices fix exactly how much it bends, through the ratio of the sines of the angles.
mechanism: Light travels at different speeds in different media — the refractive index is the ratio of its vacuum speed to its speed in the medium — and the wavefront changes direction at the boundary because one edge enters the slower medium before the other. The law can be derived either from Fermat's principle, that light takes the quickest path, or from Huygens' treatment of light as a wave.

examples.text: A straw in a glass of water looks broken at the surface because light from the submerged part refracts as it leaves the water — the everyday sight the law explains.
Curved glass surfaces refract rays to converge or diverge them, the basis of eyeglasses, cameras, and microscopes; Ibn Sahl's original use of the relationship was to design lenses.
Beyond a critical angle, light going from a denser to a thinner medium is trapped and reflected instead of refracting — the effect that guides light down optical fibres.

variants.name: Fermat's principle
variants.text: The least-time principle from which the law can be derived: light travels the path between two points that takes the least time, which forces exactly the observed bending.

variants.name: The critical angle
variants.text: The incidence angle at which the refracted ray grazes the surface; beyond it, refraction gives way entirely to total internal reflection.

whyItMatters: It is the quantitative law of refraction, the foundation of all lens and fibre optics and of how we understand rainbows, mirages, and the apparent bending of submerged objects. It is also the classic illustration of Stigler's law — named, almost arbitrarily, for one of its several independent discoverers.

working.text: predict the direction by remembering the ray bends toward the perpendicular entering a higher-index medium and away leaving it.
going from dense to thin, check whether the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, beyond which the light is totally internally reflected.
in birefringent crystals or metamaterials the simple law needs generalising, so do not assume a single refracted ray.

limits: The simple law applies cleanly to isotropic, homogeneous media. In birefringent, anisotropic crystals a ray can split into an ordinary ray that obeys it and an extraordinary ray that need not. Metamaterials with negative refractive index bend light to the same side of the perpendicular, a regime requiring a generalised formulation. As a ray-optics relation it also does not describe partial-reflection intensities, polarisation, or diffraction.
misreadings: It is a textbook Stigler's-law case: 'Snell' is historically arbitrary, since Ibn Sahl described the relationship around 984, Thomas Harriot found it in 1602, Snell derived an equivalent form in 1621 without publishing, and Descartes published it first in 1637. It also governs only isotropic media, not the split rays of birefringent crystals or negative refraction.
origin: Named for the Dutch astronomer Willebrord Snellius, who derived it around 1621 but left it unpublished. It was described by Ibn Sahl around 984, independently found by Thomas Harriot in 1602, and first published by René Descartes in 1637 — so it is called Descartes' law in France.
